entries.title: The bot in one minute
entries.short: The bot waits for price to poke through an obvious high or low, trap the late traders, then turn. It buys (or sells) the turn with a stop right behind the poke.
body: Big groups of traders park their stops and orders at obvious highs and lows. That pile of orders is [[liquidity]].
Price often runs through such a level (a [[sweep]]), traps the traders who reacted, then reverses. The bot trades that reversal.
It is one fixed set of written rules, called LIT. It trades NQ futures as [[mnq]], using [[micro]] contracts, one trade a day at most, paper only.
Every rule was picked on Jan to Jun 2026 and checked on Jul to Oct 2026.

quiz.q: What is the idea behind the bot?
quiz.a: Trade the turn after price pokes through an obvious high or low and traps traders
wrong: Buy every dip in the morning
Follow the news and trade the headline

entries.title: Step 1: mark the levels
entries.short: Before anything happens, the bot lists the obvious highs and lows: session highs and lows, yesterday, last week, last month, opening gaps, equal highs or lows.
body: Asia, London and New York [[session]] highs and lows count, once their box has closed.
[[pdh]] and PDL (yesterday), the week and the month high and low count.
The weekly and daily opening gaps count, and so do "equal lows": two swing lows at the same price, untouched in between.
A level is marked before the [[sweep]], never after. Marking it afterwards would be cheating the test.

entries.title: Step 2: wait for a sweep
entries.short: Price makes a new 2-hour low (or high) and runs through a marked level (a [[sweep]]) by at least half an [[atr]].
body: A swept low sets up a long (buy). A swept high sets up a short (sell). Shorts are the mirror image of everything here.
Half an ATR is the filter that stops tiny pokes from counting.

entries.title: Step 3: the trap (inducement)
entries.short: Just before the [[sweep]] a small swing low sat a little above the level. The final push ran through it, so early buyers got stopped out: that is the [[inducement]].
body: The small swing is at most 1 [[atr]] above the level and at most 3 hours old.
Nothing may touch it until the last push into the low.

entries.title: Step 4: the shift (5m CISD)
entries.short: Price must close back above the start of the last fall. That close is the [[cisd]], proof the sellers lost control. One strong candle on the way ([[displacement]]) is required.
body: The CISD level is the open of the first candle of the last run of down-closing 5-minute candles.
One candle body must be at least 0.8 [[atr]] (that is the displacement).
The bot only looks for entries between 02:00 and 15:30 New York time.

quiz.q: In the bot's rules, which hours can a new trade start?

entries.title: Step 5: the entry
entries.short: A buy [[limit-order]] sits at the CISD level for 30 minutes. After price taps it, the bot waits for a small 1-minute [[cisd]], then buys.
body: Once price taps the limit, the bot gives it up to 20 one-minute candles to confirm.
The setup is dropped if the [[sweep]] low breaks, the target trades first, 30 minutes pass with no tap, or it is 15:55.
The bot never chases with a market order. A missed move stays missed.

entries.title: Step 6: the stop
entries.short: The [[stop]] goes 1 [[tick]] beyond the extreme of the [[sweep]], never a fixed distance. Under 8 points or over 80 points means no trade.
body: The sweep extreme is the high or low made before the turn. If price goes back through it, the idea was wrong, so you are out.
A wide stop means fewer [[micro]] contracts (less risk). A small stop allows more. Size follows the stop.

quiz.q: Where does the bot put its stop?

entries.title: Step 7: the target
entries.short: The target is the 18:00 open plus (long) or minus (short) one day's expected move from the [[vix-band]]. It must be at least 1.5R away, and profit is banked at 8R.
body: One move = yesterday's VIX close divided by 100, divided by the square root of 252, times the 18:00 open.
Closer than 1.5[[r]] means no trade. Further than 8R means take the money at 8R. No greed.

quiz.q: Where does the bot bank profit at most?

entries.title: Step 8: manage the trade
entries.short: At +1R the stop moves to [[breakeven]] (plus 1.25 points for costs). A trade that is not working 15 minutes after the fill is closed early. Everything is flat by 15:55.
body: Breakeven: after +1R the stop goes to entry + 1.25 points, so a breakeven exit does not lose the costs.
15-minute check: if the trade never reached +0.5R and is more than 0.3R under water, it is closed at the next 1-minute open.
Flat by 15:55 New York time. MFFU needs you flat by 16:10, so there is a safety gap.
Adding to a winner ([[scale-in]]) is built but OFF until a Sim test passes.

entries.title: Step 9: the size
entries.short: Size follows the stop: about $800 of risk up to a 20-point stop, then less as the stop gets wider. Evals use a special size so one winner can pass.
body: $800 risk up to a 20-point stop, then 800 x 20 / stop. A 40-point stop risks $400, an 80-point stop $200.
[[micro]] count = risk / (stop x $2), rounded down, at most 40. Under 1 micro means no trade.
After 2 stop-outs in a week the size is halved for the rest of that week (outside the eval sizing).

entries.title: One trade a day
entries.short: The bot takes one trade a day at most, and never two at once. Expect 2 to 4 trades a week.
body: Fewer than 2 a week is too slow for an eval. The rule is: never make a filter that pauses trading for weeks.
A quiet day with no setup is normal. It is not a bug.

entries.title: Eval size: one winner passes
entries.short: In an eval the bot buys enough [[micro]] contracts that one winning trade to its target reaches the +$3,000 goal, but never risks more than 80% of the room to the floor.
body: The target is known at entry, so the bot can work out how many micros one winner needs.
A full stop-out must stay inside 80% of the room and inside the $1,000 daily loss.
The cost: about 1 eval in 5 fails within 2 weeks. The gain: most evals are decided within 2 weeks.
Near the target the size shrinks by itself.

entries.title: Funded size
entries.short: On a funded account the bot risks 60% of the room to the floor, at most $1,500 a trade, and a winner is capped at $2,000.
body: The cap on a winner is one full payout request.
When one [[micro]] could reach the floor, the bot skips.

entries.title: Paper only, you go live
entries.short: The bot trades paper (simulated) money. It never arms live trading for you. Going live on the eval is your own decision and MFFU needs you present.
body: No real order is placed unless you switch it on yourself.
Keys and secrets never go in the repo or in chat.

entries.title: How good is it? The headline
entries.short: 2026 so far: [[pf]] 4.19, +$43,820 on paper with costs in. The honest number to expect is the later half: PF 2.91, +$9,919 (about $2,670 a month).
body: Quote the Jul to Oct check, not the best-looking number. It was not used to pick the rules.
PF 2.91 means every $1 lost was matched by $2.91 won.
2021 to 2025 is only a reference line. The bot is tuned and judged on 2026.

quiz.q: Which result should you quote as the one to expect?
quiz.a: The Jul to Oct check, PF 2.91

entries.title: Money, not only R
entries.short: Every result shows net dollars and dollars a month next to [[pf]] and [[r]]. R alone hides how much real money is at stake.
body: Eval prices you pay: Builder 50K $91.80, Builder 25K $63, one-time, $0 activation. Not the list price.
On funded accounts you keep 80% of each payout.

entries.title: Eval speed: 2 weeks
entries.short: An eval should be passed or failed within 2 weeks (10 sessions) and never take more than 3 weeks to pass.
body: Each run shows p10 and f10 (passed or failed within 10 sessions), the share decided in 10, and the median sessions to pass.
On the Jul to Oct check, 58.6% passed and 20.9% failed within 2 weeks.

entries.title: Two halves rule
entries.short: A rule change is only kept if it also works on the second half of the data it was not picked on.
body: Pick on Jan to Jun 2026, check on Jul to Oct 2026, report both.
This is how the bot avoids fooling itself with luck.

entries.title: The drawdown floor
entries.short: Your account fails if your balance, with any open trade, touches the floor. On the 50K the floor starts at $48,000.
body: The floor only moves up, and only at the end of the day, from your best end-of-day balance (this is [[eod-trailing]]).
It stops at $50,100 (start + $100) and stays there.
An open loss counts the moment it happens, not at the close.
The room to the floor is what the bot sizes against.

quiz.q: On the Builder 50K, what happens if your balance touches the floor?
wrong: You are paused for the day

entries.title: The daily loss limit
entries.short: On the 50K the daily loss limit is $1,000. It is soft: hit it and you are paused for the session, but the account stays open.
body: The bot keeps every full stop-out inside this number.
The Builder 25K limit is $600.

entries.title: The profit target
entries.short: The 50K eval passes at +$3,000. There is no [[consistency]] rule in the eval. The 25K needs +$1,500.
body: There is no time limit counting down on the eval. The 7-day inactivity rule still applies.

entries.title: How many contracts
entries.short: The 50K allows 40 micros or 4 minis, counted together: 10 micros = 1 mini. The 25K allows 20 micros.
body: Over the limit, the order is rejected.
A [[micro]] is the small contract.

entries.title: Flat by 16:10
entries.short: Trading is intraday only. You must be flat by 16:10 New York time and no weekend holds. The bot is flat by 15:55 to be safe.
body: The platform closes you at 16:10. Never force orders after it.

quiz.q: MFFU needs you flat by what time?

entries.title: No long and short at once
entries.short: You may not hold a long and a short on the same market at the same time, also across your accounts.
body: That is why one strategy always has priority when two want opposite sides.

entries.title: Bots are allowed
entries.short: Bots are allowed with your own settings and you watching. No high-frequency trading and no exploiting simulated fills.
body: MFFU requires you to be present for live trading.

entries.title: News
entries.short: News is allowed in the eval and on a sim-funded account. On a live account MFFU advises against trading it.

entries.title: The 7-day rule
entries.short: Trade at least once every 7 days or the account can be closed.
body: The bot normally trades 2 to 4 times a week, so this only matters in a quiet or holiday week.

quiz.q: How often must you trade so the account is not closed?

entries.title: Payouts
entries.short: On a funded account the first payout opens once you are $500 above the $2,100 [[buffer]], so a balance of $52,600. Payouts run $500 to $2,000, and 80% is yours.
body: Your best day must stay under 50% of the cycle's profit ([[consistency]]).
After 5 sim payouts the account moves to live.
Check MFFU's own pages before asking for a payout. The rules were last checked on 2026-10-18.

quiz.q: What share of each payout is yours?

entries.title: What the evals cost you
entries.short: You paid $91.80 for the Builder 50K and $63 for the Builder 25K. One-time payment, no activation fee, no monthly renewal.
body: List prices are higher. Always use your real price when comparing.

entries.title: The graveyard: 19 lists of dead ends
entries.short: Many ideas were tested properly and dropped. Before you suggest a new strategy idea, search here first.
body: Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.
The rule for keeping an idea: better in 2026 and better in 2021 to 2025, and still 2 or more trades a week.

entries.title: Famous models as taught
entries.short: ICT 2022, Silver Bullet, Mech/IFVG and similar models, traded exactly as taught, made 0.2 to 1.5 trades a week and a [[pf]] near 1 (break-even).
body: That is why the bot has its own rules, written down and tested with costs.
IFVG is explained here: [[ifvg]]. The bot uses a simpler signal.
Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.

entries.title: More confluences (92 tried)
entries.short: 92 extra confirmations, 6 ways to guess the daily bias, and sizing by trade "grade" were tested. None held up.
body: Adding conditions made trades rarer without making them better. Partials and trailing stops also failed.

entries.title: Fixed small stops
entries.short: Stops of a fixed 10 to 15 points got wicked out and lost money. Real structure stops are rarely that small.
body: Your own principle: the stop sits at the protected low or high, never a random distance.

entries.title: Other targets
entries.short: No cap, "draw on liquidity" and "last real pool" targets all did worse (profit factor 1.6 to 2.2 against 3.48).
body: The single VIX-band target banked at 8R stayed.

entries.title: Skip after a cold streak
entries.short: A filter that stops trading after losers had the best profit factor, but paused trading for 14 weeks. You rejected it.
body: Rule: prefer a size change over skipping. Never pause for weeks.

entries.title: The LIT extras (none adopted)
entries.short: Order blocks, higher-timeframe confluences, other hours, extra continuation trades, looser filters and other markets were tested in hundreds of variants. None held in both halves.
body: Two small upgrades did pass and are ON: the 15-minute check and [[breakeven]] with costs.
Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.

entries.title: Fancier exits
entries.short: Exit on a sharp reversal, trailing behind swings, and [[breakeven]] at other points: 103 variants, none better in both halves.
body: Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.

entries.title: A second strategy alone
entries.short: Breakout and intraday-momentum ideas were real but too weak to pass a prop eval alone. They only work as a small add-on.
body: Prop rules (floor, 50% best day) punish strategies with long losing runs.

entries.title: Structure-based management
entries.short: Targets at the next pool, half off early, stops to protected swings, trend filters: 101 variants. None beat the live rules in both halves.
body: One lead is being watched (a 15-minute structure trail after +1R) but it is not switched on.

entries.title: Skipping LIT to protect a second account
entries.short: Letting the second account (ATLAS) block LIT's opposite trade made the 2021 to 2025 result worse. LIT keeps priority.
body: Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.

entries.title: A scalper like a person
entries.short: A fast scalping strategy on its own 25K account, with many exit and filter ideas (about 2,000 variants), did not beat today's rule.
body: Do not redo it unless you have a genuinely new idea.

ask.a: Price runs through a level of liquidity, takes the orders there, then often turns around.

entries.title: Displacement

entries.title: When... I have a loss
entries.short: A stop-out is a normal cost of the system, not a mistake. Do nothing special: no revenge trade, no bigger size.
body: 1. Check the stop was hit where the rules say (1 tick beyond the [[sweep]] extreme). If yes, it worked as designed.
2. Do not change any rule because of one loss or one bad week. Rules change only with two-halves proof.
3. After 2 stop-outs in a week the size halves by itself (outside the eval).
4. If the account is near the [[floor]], look at the room left before the next trade; the bot shrinks size by itself.
5. Tell the chat if something looks off. It checks the trade against the bot's twin.

entries.title: When... two losses in a row
entries.short: A short losing run is expected. The system's worst runs in testing were still inside the limits. Keep the size the bot gives you.
body: Never double up to win it back.
Never skip trades by hand because you feel unsure: skipping the one winner is the real cost.

entries.title: When... 7 days with no trade
entries.short: The account can be closed after 7 days with no trade. Watch the calendar in a quiet or holiday week.
body: 1. Count days since the last fill. Warn yourself at day 5.
2. Tell the chat at day 5 so it can check for a real setup or a feed problem.
3. Do not force a big trade just to reset the clock. Keep size small and inside the rules.
4. A "feed stale" message means the bot will not enter. Fix the feed rather than guessing.

entries.title: When... an eval fails
entries.short: A fail costs the eval fee ($91.80). About 1 eval in 5 fails within 2 weeks by design: the fast size accepts that for speed.
body: 1. Do not panic and do not change the rules. A fail is in the numbers.
2. Buy the next eval (no reset price is published for one-time plans; check the MFFU dashboard).
3. Tell the chat the new start date so the session count starts fresh.
4. Look for a code or fill problem first, but expect it to be normal variance.

entries.title: When... an eval passes
entries.short: You hit +$3,000. Stop trading the eval and move the account to funded.
body: 1. Do not keep trading the eval after the target.
2. Tell the chat so the funded size (60% of the room, at most $1,500) is switched on.
3. Funded rules differ: payouts need a buffer and a best-day check.

entries.title: When... I want a payout
entries.short: Check three things before you ask: balance, buffer, best day.
body: 1. Your balance is at least $52,600 for the first payout ($2,100 buffer + $500).
2. Your best day is under 50% of the cycle's profit ([[consistency]]).
3. Ask for between $500 and $2,000. You get 80%.
4. Re-check MFFU's own payout page that day. Rules change.
5. After 5 sim payouts the account moves to live, and you must be present to trade it.

entries.title: When... I hit the daily loss limit
entries.short: You are paused for the session, not failed. Stop for the day.
body: 1. Do not try to trade it back.
2. Check that the account is not also close to the floor.
3. Come back next session with the normal size.

entries.title: When... I want to go live
entries.short: Going live is only ever your decision. The bot is paper only and never arms live trading for you.
body: 1. MFFU requires you to be present for live trading.
2. Run the Sim test first and read the go-live checklist.
3. Start with the smallest size.

entries.title: When... I want to try a new idea
entries.short: Search the rejected list first. Then test it on both halves with costs and 2 or more trades a week.
body: Keep it only if it is better in 2026 and in 2021 to 2025.
Ask the chat to run it. Do not change live rules by hand.

entries.title: Jarvis: the home app
entries.short: Jarvis is your home screen app. You see a greeting, the NQ market line and a card for each of your apps. You can type to it or talk to it.
body: The round orb in the corner jumps you to any other OLYMPUS app.
Without any key it answers from your own numbers: status, room left to the floor, today's P&L, "open Zenith".
It never places a trade. It reads and it opens things.
Open it when: you start the day, or want any answer fast.
The one thing to look at: the short list of what needs you first. Urgent things come first.

entries.title: Jarvis modes
entries.short: Jarvis has five modes: Auto, Trading, Research, Business and Life. A mode changes the quick questions, which apps show first and how Jarvis thinks.
body: Switch with the chips above the quick questions, or say "switch to research mode".
Auto (the default) picks the mode from the words of your question.

Trading = the bots, the room left and the plan. Research = Data City, Prometheus, DAPHNE and the Mind. Business = money goal, more accounts, Kalshi, to-dos with deadlines. Life = Planner and reminders.
Open it when: you switch from trading to studying or planning.
The one thing to look at: the quick questions change with the mode.

entries.title: Jarvis: Think for me
entries.short: Tap Think for me (or say "think for me" or "what would you do") and Jarvis gives you 3 ideas of what to do next, most urgent first.
body: With no key it uses rules over your numbers: the 7-day rule, room left, a stale feed, due to-dos, a reminder soon, tomorrow's plan.
With a free key a model writes the 3 ideas instead. If anything fails, the rules answer.
Every idea is an ask, an open or a mode switch. It is never a trade.
Open it when: you do not know what to do next.
The one thing to look at: the first idea. It is the urgent one.

entries.title: Jarvis: talking
entries.short: Jarvis speaks every answer out loud by default, and you can talk to it when your phone allows the mic. There is a speaker toggle to turn the voice off.
body: On iPhone the first tap unlocks the sound. After that it can speak.
If the mic is not allowed (common in a Home Screen app) there is a type-to-talk field instead.
The Voice sheet lists the voices, best first. See [[o-phone]] for the best voice.
Open it when: your hands are busy.
The one thing to look at: the speaker toggle, if you want it quiet.

entries.title: Jarvis: smart mode (free key)
entries.short: Smart mode makes Jarvis answer anything, not only your numbers. It needs a free key from Groq, Gemini or OpenRouter. The setup screen walks you through it.
body: 1. In Jarvis tap the three dots, then AI key, then Free key setup. (Or say "set up smart mode".)
2. Pick Groq, Gemini or OpenRouter. Each tab has 3 steps and a button to the key page.
3. Paste the key and tap Test. It saves only after Jarvis got an answer.
The key stays on your phone and is only sent to the company you chose. Never paste it in chat.
Open it when: you want questions answered that your numbers cannot answer.
The one thing to look at: the Test result.

quiz.q: Where does your smart mode key live?

entries.title: Jarvis and Obsidian notes
entries.short: Jarvis reads your Obsidian notes, answers from them and adds to them, but only after you say yes. It is free.
body: Set up once (about 5 minutes): install the Git plugin in Obsidian, make a private GitHub repo named obsidian-vault, make a token with Contents read and write for that repo.
Then in Jarvis: three dots, Obsidian, paste the repo and the token, Connect.
Say "what did I write about drawdown", "open tasks" or "today's daily note". Say "note: ..." to save one. It asks first.
Open it when: you want to write something down or find something you wrote.
The one thing to look at: the yes or no question before it saves.

entries.title: Zenith: the phone dashboard
entries.short: Zenith is the dashboard that runs even when the PC is off. It shows the bots' state, today's result, the equity curve against the drawdown floor and the next trading window.
body: It is read-only and paper first. It never places or changes a trade.
It refreshes when the cloud monitor runs, so a number can be a few minutes old.
Open it when: you want the full picture of the bots, trades and results.
The one thing to look at: the equity curve and how far it sits above the drawdown floor ([[floor]]).

entries.title: Oracle: the live radar
entries.short: Oracle is a live 3D radar of NQ. It draws the bot's levels, the sweeps, which stage the bot is in and its position.
body: Look at the levels it draws: they are the same levels the strategy marks (see [[step-1]]).
Open it when: you want to see what the bot is waiting for right now.
The one thing to look at: the stage the bot is in, and whether it holds a position.

entries.title: Odeon: trade replays
entries.short: Odeon replays the bots' trades as a 3D film, bar by bar, with captions. Each trade is a reel.
body: The card in Jarvis shows the number of reels and the net of all of them.
Open it when: a trade is done and you want to see how it played out.
The one thing to look at: the caption on the latest reel: the result in dollars and in [[r]].

entries.title: Fates: your odds
entries.short: Fates runs a Monte Carlo (many simulated futures) on the bots' own results and shows how likely an eval is to pass, to fail, and what a month is worth. Paper only.
body: It is a simulation of the past. It is not a promise.
Open it when: you start a new eval, or wonder how risky it is.
The one thing to look at: the pass odds and the fail odds next to each other.

entries.title: Data City: tested ideas
entries.short: Data City draws every tested time of day, confluence and market state as a building. It is the machine that tests ideas against the data.
body: Before you suggest an idea, look at [[x-all]]. Many ideas died here.
Open it when: you are curious what was tested, or you have a new idea.
The one thing to look at: how many buildings pass the noise guard, and how many a placebo test lets through.

entries.title: DAPHNE: the strategy tree
entries.short: DAPHNE searches a tree of rules. Each branch adds one condition to a plain level trade. It cuts branches that cannot win and tests the best path on data it never saw.
body: Today's card says the top rules are no better than chance, so nothing changes in the bot.
Open it when: you want to know if a rule idea holds up.
The one thing to look at: the out-of-sample result. If it is no better than chance, it is paper only.

entries.title: Prometheus: evolving the bot
entries.short: Prometheus breeds many versions of the live strategy's settings and checks each survivor on data it was not bred on.
body: Nothing it finds changes the bot by itself.
Open it when: you wonder if the live settings can be improved.
The one thing to look at: does the champion still win on the second half (H2). If it drops, the live settings stay.

entries.title: Pantheon: the market mood
entries.short: Pantheon collects free market data (liquidity, rates, volatility, the calendar, the dollar, credit, crypto), one Greek god per source, and ends with a Council verdict.
body: It is context only. The bot does not use it to trade.
Open it when: before the session, for the big picture.
The one thing to look at: the Council verdict, for example Mixed 44 out of 100.

entries.title: Planner: your calendar
entries.short: Planner is your calendar. Jarvis reads it for the day's card and for reminders.
body: On iPhone each Home Screen app keeps its own storage, so link the Planner's sync once inside Jarvis.
Open it when: you plan the day or the week.
The one thing to look at: what is due today.

entries.title: Mind: your notes as a brain
entries.short: Mind shows your Obsidian notes and Jarvis's memory as a living 3D brain.
body: Open it when: you want to see what you have been thinking about.
The one thing to look at: the big clusters: they are the themes of your notes.

entries.title: Arena: ranks and labours
entries.short: Arena gives you XP, ranks, 12 Labours, daily quests and streaks. XP comes only from things that can be checked, like the bots running.
body: It is a game layer over real events. Paper only.
Open it when: you want a small goal for the day.
The one thing to look at: today's quests.

entries.title: Kalshi: the other bot
entries.short: The Kalshi page shows your Kalshi bot's balance, profit, open bets with their edge, the size it uses and how well its odds were right.
body: The page only shows numbers the bot's server sends. It is a separate bot with real money, and it lives on its own server.
Open it when: you want to check the Kalshi bot.
The one thing to look at: balance and today's profit.

entries.title: Tyche: Kalshi as a wheel
entries.short: Tyche draws the Kalshi bot's bets as a wheel of fortune. Open bets orbit as coins. Wins fall into the gold fountain.
body: It is read-only.
Open it when: you want a fun look at the Kalshi bot.
The one thing to look at: the coins that are still open.

entries.title: Hermes: your week
entries.short: Hermes (Wrapped) tells the week of the bots as stories: net dollars, dollars a month, the best and worst trade, evals and discipline.
body: Open it when: on Friday evening or the weekend.
The one thing to look at: the net for the week and the best trade.

entries.title: Bridge: working with ChatGPT
entries.short: Bridge is a page of jobs you can hand to ChatGPT (art, text, bulk work). Claude does the engine, the tests and the publishing.
body: It never touches the bots. ChatGPT only adds files in a folder called handoff/inbox.
Open it when: you want ChatGPT to make something for OLYMPUS.
The one thing to look at: the list of job cards.

entries.title: Bridge: the ChatGPT sync steps
entries.short: Paste the onboarding text into ChatGPT once. After that ChatGPT and Claude stay in step through one GitHub repo.
body: 1. One time: open handoff/ONBOARD.md in the repo and paste it into ChatGPT.
2. Copy a job card from the Bridge page and give it to ChatGPT.
3. ChatGPT builds it and adds the files under handoff/inbox/<job>/ in a pull request. It never edits the bots.
4. Tell Claude "Bridge: <job> done". Claude checks it, wires it in and ships it.
Rules for ChatGPT: paper only, no keys or logins, no changes to the engine or live settings.
Open it when: you want ChatGPT to build something.
The one thing to look at: the job card you copy.

entries.title: Ares: the war room
entries.short: Ares is the checklist and the risk calculator. You type the entry and the stop and it says GO, WAIT or HALT and how many contracts fit.
body: Size follows the stop: a wide stop means fewer contracts.
Open it when: before you place any trade by hand.
The one thing to look at: the verdict: GO, WAIT or HALT.

entries.title: Plutus: the money plan
entries.short: Plutus shows how many prop accounts you could run, what they cost, when payouts land and what a month is worth. Sliders, no promises.
body: 2021 to 2025 is shown as a reference only.
Open it when: you plan more accounts or wonder about money.
The one thing to look at: dollars a month on the later half of the data (Jul to Oct).

entries.title: Athena: this library
entries.short: Athena is this library. Search it, tap a shelf, read the playbooks or take the quiz.
body: Quiz me gives 5 questions from the library and saves nothing.
Open it when: you forget a rule or a word, or something happens and you want the playbook.
The one thing to look at: the search box: type one word.

entries.title: Phone setup
entries.short: Add each OLYMPUS app to your Home Screen, close and reopen it after an update, and pick the best voice for Jarvis.
body: 1. Open the page in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. Do it for Jarvis, and for any app you use a lot.
2. After an update, fully close OLYMPUS (swipe it away) and reopen it so the new version loads.
3. A white or black screen means the page did not load. Delete the icon and add it again from Safari.
4. Voice tip: Settings, then Accessibility, then Spoken Content, then Voices, then Ava (Premium). Download it and Jarvis sounds better.
5. Each Home Screen app keeps its own storage, so connect the Planner, your key and Obsidian inside Jarvis once.
Main page: https://demetrades2000-coder.github.io/nq-dashboard/ (Jarvis is at /jarvis/).

quiz.q: Where do you get the best Jarvis voice on iPhone?
quiz.a: Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content, Voices, Ava (Premium)

entries.title: Daily routine
entries.short: A simple day: look before the session, leave the bot alone during it, review after. Three short steps each.
body: BEFORE the session: 1. Open Jarvis and read the first item on its list. 2. Check the bot is on and its feed is not stale in [[o-zenith]]. 3. Check days since the last trade (the [[m-idle]] rule) and the room left to the [[floor]].
DURING: 1. Let the bot trade. New entries can start from 02:00 to 15:30 New York time. 2. Watch in [[o-oracle]] if you like, but change nothing. 3. Do not trade by hand without [[o-ares]] saying GO.

AFTER: 1. Everything is flat by 15:55. Look at the result in [[o-zenith]]. 2. If a trade closed, watch it in [[o-odeon]]. 3. Write one line in your notes (say "note: ..." to Jarvis) and read tomorrow's plan.
If something looks wrong, tell the chat. Do not change settings yourself.
